messages.author: c21e804e07c5e732
messages.subject: Plot multiple two dimensional data
parts:
I know that I could do the following in the traditional way to plot
multiple two dimensional data.

plot(x1,y1)
points(x2,y2)

, where x1, y1, x2 and y2 are all vectors.

I could combine the vectors into a data.frame and add one additional
column to see where each row is coming from (1 or 2). So that I can
use qplot(..., shape=additional_column).

But this is tedious. I'm wondering what is the most convenient way to
do so in ggplot2. Thank you!

messages.author: 260e37e157eb3823
messages.subject: Re: Plot multiple two dimensional data
parts:
Peng,

the only way I can think of is to do exactly what you described and
combine everything in a single data frame. That makes it also much
cleaner:

df$x <- c(x1,x2)
df$y <- c(y1,y2)
df$part <- rep(c(1,2), c(length(x1), length(x2))

qplot(x,y, geom="point", colour=factor(part), data=df)

Heike

While Heike's code is a little bit longer than your code, it also does
a lot more:

* adds a legend to distinguish the two groups
* ensures that the scales are cover both data sets
* makes it much easier to add additional summaries of the data

And it works with a much more precise description of the data.
Typically if you have a whole lot of random vectors floating around
your workspace, it indicates that you're not managing your data very
well at a higher level - like things should be grouped together in the
same data frame.

To an end user, he/she doesn't care about how the data is combined.
Maybe the combination code can be somehow encapsulated under a unified
grammar interface? For example,

new_plot(x1, x2, y1, y2, type='shape')

This means that the two data set will be distinguished by 'shape'. By
this way, the user can plot arbitrary number of data sets. For
example, the following command means to distinguish the data sets by
both shape and color.

new_plot(x1, x2, y1, y2, z1, z2, type=c('shape', 'color'))

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Plot multiple two dimensional data
parts:
Hi,

well you could define your own function to do the dirty work of
wrapping up the data, something like this perhaps,


pairstodf <- function(..., groupname=NULL){

dots <- list(...)
n <- length(dots)
if(n %% 2) stop("input should be have an even number")

pairs <- list()
for (ii in seq(1, n-1, by=2)){
pairs[[(ii+1)/2]] <- data.frame(x=dots[[ii]], y=dots[[ii+1]])
}

if(!is.null(groupname)) attr(pairs, "varname") <- groupname
melt(pairs, id="x")

}

x1 <- seq(1, 10)
x2 <- seq(1, 10)
y1 <- rnorm(10)
y2 <- runif(10)

pairstodf(x1, y1, x2, y2)

pairstodf(x1, y1, x2, y2, groupname = "mygroup")


HTH,

baptiste

parts: > To an end user, he/she doesn't care about how the data is combined.

My point is that they should care - they should care very much. The
way that data is stored is critically important for all sorts of
processing in r and I very strongly believe that data preparation and
visualisation should be kept quite separate. Qplot is my one
compromise for convenience.
